title: Migrant Children Risk Losing Legal Representation as Federal Aid Contract Expires
excerpt: More than 26,000 unaccompanied children could face immigration courts without lawyers as the Trump administration moves to end the program, despite court orders to maintain funding.
body:
• More than 26,000 unaccompanied migrant children are at risk of losing their court-appointed attorneys as the Trump administration moves to end the federal contract funding their legal representation.
  • A federal judge issued a preliminary injunction requiring continued funding, but the administration has argued taxpayers have no obligation to cover legal aid costs for migrant children.
  • Without representation, children are five to six times less likely to succeed in their immigration cases, according to legal aid organizations.
  • The Trafficking Victims Protection Reauthorization Act of 2008 requires the government to ensure legal counsel for unaccompanied children.

Children Facing Courts Alone

Children so young their feet cannot touch the floor when they sit in courtroom chairs are at risk of losing their legal representation in immigration court, as the Trump administration presses forward with plans to end a federal contract that funds attorneys for unaccompanied minors.

The contract, managed through the Acacia Center for Justice, had supported a network of 89 legal services organizations nationally. Collectively, they represent more than 26,000 children with cases before immigration courts and provide consultations and referrals to thousands more each year.

A Legal Battle Over Funding

On March 21, the administration notified nonprofit legal aid groups that it would terminate the contract. Eleven subcontractor organizations sued, and a federal judge in California issued a preliminary injunction requiring the government to continue funding.

Judge Araceli Martínez-Olguín noted in her ruling that Congress has consistently appropriated funds to represent children in immigration proceedings. She said the nonprofits raised serious questions about whether the administration's actions violated its obligations under the Trafficking Victims Protection Reauthorization Act of 2008.

"Immigrants are five to six times more likely to succeed in their case if they're represented by an attorney. If they lose representation, that's going to be really damaging for their case."

— Joel Frost-Tift, Immigration Attorney, Public Counsel

The Human Cost

Many of these children do not read or speak English. Some are too young to read or speak at all. They arrived in the United States fleeing violence, sexual abuse, and neglect in their home countries, often without parents or guardians.

Legal aid organizations say the loss of funding would leave children to navigate one of the most complex legal systems in the country on their own. Without attorneys, children are more likely to miss hearings, lose connections to service providers, and receive deportation orders.

Beyond their legal cases, these children are enrolled in school, some hold jobs to cover basic living expenses, and many require therapy to process traumas from their home countries and their journeys to the United States.

Uncertain Future

The administration has argued that taxpayers have no obligation to pay the cost of direct legal aid to migrant children. Attorneys for the government also contend that district courts have no jurisdiction over a contract termination.

Meanwhile, many legal aid organizations continue to represent children in court given their ethical and professional obligations, even without government funding. But without new funding, it remains unclear how long they can sustain this work.

The case highlights the broader tension within the administration's immigration enforcement priorities: the push to reduce costs and accelerate deportations against the legal protections specifically designed to safeguard the most vulnerable individuals in the system.
nri_angle: Indian American immigration attorneys and community organizations are among those advocating for continued legal protections, as some unaccompanied South Asian minors are among those at risk of losing representation.
